children.text: The way back
Name the bus stop or ferry wharf where the walk ends, and check the timetable on the day before you set off.
Saltwater is a guide to Sydney's coastal walks, from Bondi to the Royal National Park. Each walk is walked, timed and written up, with where to swim at the end, and updated each season.
How we write a walk

Every walk opens with its distance, how long it took us and how you get home. The times are ours, walking steadily with stops for photos; add time for swims and for the stairs. Each walk shows when we last walked it and what had changed since.
What we do not check
Tracks close after storms, in fire weather and for repairs, and pools are drained for cleaning. Check NSW National Parks and the local council for closures before you go.
Credits

Made by the Pinies in Piny, on EmDash. Walked and checked by people. Photos on Unsplash and the video on Pexels, by Dominic Kurniawan Suryaputra, Gary Runn, Matt Str, Steven Zhang, Kelvin Li, Colton Jones, Jack Bass and Edan Kwon.
Sydney's coast is easy walking on a calm day and a different place in a big swell or a heatwave. Read this before you head out.
The swell
Over two metres, rock pools and low ledges close. We say so at the top of each walk. Waves on this coast come in sets, and a quiet ledge can be washed over without warning.
The heat
Most of these walks have no shade. Go early, carry two litres, and wear a hat.
The way back
Every walk ends at a bus stop or a ferry wharf, and we name it. Check the timetable before you set off.
Updated
Each walk shows when we last walked it and what had changed. Conditions change faster than we can walk them, so check the park and council alerts on the day.

data.title: Bondi to Coogee
data.excerpt: Sydney's best-loved walk: six kilometres of headlands, ocean pools and beaches, with a swim at either end.

$media.alt: A walker on the sandstone cliffs south of Bondi

children.text: 6 km · 2–3 hours · Easy, with stairs · Bus back from Coogee.

If you only walk one stretch of Sydney's coast, make it this one. The path leaves the south end of Bondi Beach beside the Icebergs pool and keeps to the cliff edge, dropping into a beach or a cove every kilometre or so before it climbs out again.
The route

From Bondi the path rounds Mackenzies Point to Tamarama, a small, steep beach known for strong rips. Bronte comes next, with its park, its rock baths and a line of cafés behind the sand. Past Bronte the path runs beside Waverley Cemetery, high above the water, before it comes down to Clovelly, a long narrow inlet that is calm on most days.

After Clovelly the path goes around Gordons Bay, where the water is clear enough for snorkelling on a flat day, and then along the last headland into Coogee. The walk is short, but the stairs add up: count on climbing out of every beach.
Where to swim

There are ocean pools along the way and a beach at each end. Bondi Icebergs at the start charges entry; Bronte's rock baths are free. Swim between the flags on the beaches, and treat the pools as closed when waves are washing over their walls.
The way back
Buses run from Coogee back towards Bondi Junction and the city. Check the stop and the timetable before you set off, because the walk takes longer than it looks once you stop to swim.
Start early, swim at the end, and the bus home feels like a reward.
Last walked this spring: the Tamarama stairs were open, and Bronte pool was drained for cleaning.

data.title: Spit to Manly
data.excerpt: Ten kilometres of harbour bush, small beaches and sandstone headlands, from the Spit Bridge to the Manly ferry.

$media.alt: Sandstone cliffs at North Head, Manly

children.text: 10 km · 3–4 hours · Moderate · Ferry back from Manly.

This is the harbour's long walk, and it feels much further from the city than it is. The track starts at the northern end of the Spit Bridge and follows the shore of Middle Harbour all the way to Manly Cove, mostly through bush, with sandy beaches and rock shelves in between.
The route

The first stretch runs past Clontarf, a family beach with a netted swimming area. The track then climbs onto the headlands, where there are rough sections over sandstone and roots, and stairs in both directions. Grotto Point has a small lighthouse and, nearby, Aboriginal rock engravings; stay on the boardwalk and leave them as you find them.

From Dobroyd Head you look across the harbour mouth to North Head, the cliffs in the photograph. The track then drops past Reef Beach, Forty Baskets and Fairlight, and the last kilometre into Manly is an easy path along the water.
Where to swim
Clontarf and Forty Baskets are both sheltered; Forty Baskets has a small tidal pool. The water at Manly Cove is calm, and the ocean beach is a short walk across the Corso if you want waves.
The way back
Ferries run from Manly Wharf to Circular Quay. Sit outside on the way back: the ride across the harbour is the walk seen from the water.

data.title: South Head
data.excerpt: A short loop from Watsons Bay to Hornby Lighthouse, the red and white tower at the harbour's southern gate.

children.text: 1.5 km loop · 45 minutes · Easy.

South Head is the shortest walk here and one of the best for a first visit. The loop starts near Camp Cove, a few minutes' walk from the Watsons Bay ferry wharf, and follows a mostly flat track out to the point.
The route

The path passes Lady Bay and the old gun emplacements that once guarded the harbour, then reaches Hornby Lighthouse, painted in red and white stripes so ships could see it by day. From the point you look straight across to North Head, with the open ocean on one side and the harbour on the other.
The track has had repairs; our new photos are from the walk after they were finished. Some sections are close to the cliff edge, so keep children close.
Where to swim
Camp Cove is a small, calm harbour beach at the start of the loop. Watsons Bay has a harbour pool and fish and chips by the water.
The way back
Ferries run from Watsons Bay to Circular Quay, and buses go back to the city.

data.title: The Coast Track
data.excerpt: Bundeena to Otford through the Royal National Park, past Wedding Cake Rock, seen from the track.

$media.alt: Wedding Cake Rock above the ocean in the Royal National Park

children.text: 26 km · 2 days · Hard · Booking needed for the campground.
The Coast Track runs the length of the Royal National Park, from Bundeena in the north to Otford in the south. It is the longest walk on this site, and the only one we split over two days.
Day one

From Bundeena the track crosses open heath along the cliff tops. Wedding Cake Rock, the white sandstone ledge in the photograph, is fenced off because it is unstable: look at it from the track and do not climb the fence. The track then reaches Wattamolla, a lagoon and beach that make a good lunch stop, and continues past Eagle Rock and the falls at Curracurrong to Garie Beach.
Day two

South of Garie the track passes the beaches of North and South Era and Burning Palms, then climbs into rainforest before the final stretch to Otford. The rock platforms along this section, including the Figure Eight Pools, are dangerous in any swell and can be cut off by the tide; we do not route the walk through them.
Planning

Camping in the park is booked through NSW National Parks, and the campground at North Era is the usual halfway stop. Carry all your water for the first day, a stove and a map. Check the park's alerts before you go, because sections of the track close after storms and in fire weather.
Getting there and back
Bundeena is reached by ferry from Cronulla. Otford has a train station on the South Coast line, a short and steep climb down from the end of the track.

data.title: Bondi to Watsons Bay
data.excerpt: North from Bondi along the cliff tops, past Diamond Bay, to fish and chips by the harbour.

$media.alt: Turquoise water below the cliffs at Diamond Bay

children.text: 6.5 km · 2.5 hours · Easy, with stairs · Ferry back from Watsons Bay.
This is the quieter half of the eastern beaches walk. It leaves the north end of Bondi Beach and follows the cliffs north to the harbour, ending at Watsons Bay instead of another beach.
The route

From North Bondi the path climbs over Ben Buckler and through the streets and reserves of Dover Heights, where some stretches are footpath rather than track. At Diamond Bay a walkway runs along the cliff top above deep, clear water. Further on, the path passes Macquarie Lighthouse and then follows the cliffs of The Gap down into Watsons Bay.
Shade
There is almost none. The cliff tops are open to the sun and the wind, and the only cover is in the reserves between them. Start early on a warm day and carry two litres of water.
Where to swim
Swim at Bondi before you start or at the harbour end: Watsons Bay has a netted harbour pool, and Camp Cove is a short walk away. The cliffs in between have no safe way down to the water.
The way back
Ferries run from Watsons Bay to Circular Quay; check the times before you set off, as they are less frequent in the evening. Buses also run back to the city.
